title: Al-Qaida: 25 Years After 9/11
gist: Twenty-five years after 9/11 the terrorism field is split over al-Qaida's relevance, but the article's position is that the group failed to deliver its promised Sunni Caliphate, was weakened by the schism that produced the Islamic State, and has been superseded by IS — with the two groups' infighting actively helping security agencies cut both down to size.

insights.claim: Twenty-five years after the September 11, 2001 attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, terrorism scholars and practitioners remain divided over al-Qaida's status, with some seeing a potent threat of a different nature and others arguing it has lost its momentum.
insights.speaker: Abdul Basit
insights.so_what: Expert disagreement on al-Qaida means counterterrorism resourcing debates remain unsettled; both narratives will continue driving policy swings.
insights.quote: the fraternity of terrorism scholars and practitioners is divided over al-Qaida’s status
insights.locator: Twenty-five years after the fateful terrorist attacks

insights.claim: Al-Qaida failed to create the Sunni global Caliphate it promised its followers, which is the core measure by which the organization should be judged a strategic failure.
insights.speaker: Abdul Basit
insights.so_what: Judge jihadist organizations against their own stated objectives rather than against attack counts; the gap erodes recruitment legitimacy.
insights.locator: Indeed, al-Qaida failed to create the Sunni global Caliphate

insights.claim: The global jihadist movement split between al-Qaida and the Islamic State, and that split weakened al-Qaida specifically.
insights.speaker: Abdul Basit
insights.so_what: Fragmentation of the jihadist movement is a structural reason for al-Qaida's decline, not merely a consequence of counterterrorism pressure.
insights.locator: the global jihadist movement split between al-Qaida and the Islamic State

insights.claim: The Islamic State has superseded al-Qaida as the dominant global jihadist actor.
insights.speaker: Abdul Basit
insights.so_what: Threat modelling and counterterrorism resourcing should be weighted toward IS and its affiliates rather than toward al-Qaida's legacy structure.
insights.quote: IS has superseded al-Qaida as the dominant global jihadist actor.

insights.claim: The ideological tussle and inter-group fighting between al-Qaida and the Islamic State have helped security and intelligence agencies around the world cut both organizations down to size.
insights.speaker: Abdul Basit
insights.so_what: Jihadist infighting functions as a force multiplier for counterterrorism; a future reconciliation or merger between the currents would be the genuine escalation signal.
insights.quote: The ideological tussle and inter-group fighting between al-Qaida and IS have helped security and intelligence agencies around the world to cut them to size.
insights.locator: The ideological tussle and inter-group fighting
